result:
There's a particular thrill in finding a stranger's handwriting in a used book. A name on the flyleaf—Margaret Ellison, 1962—or a penciled underline beneath a sentence someone, decades ago, decided mattered. Sometimes just a single exclamation point in the margin, emphatic and anonymous, and you're left wondering what thought detonated there. Once, a grocery list used as a bookmark: milk, batteries, "call Ruth." I hope Ruth got the call.

Marginalia is a conversation across time, though a one-sided one. The original reader never hears your objections. I once bought a battered copy of Marcus Aurelius in which someone had argued with nearly every paragraph—furious little question marks, one deeply sarcastic "oh, easy for HIM to say." I disagreed with the annotator constantly, which meant, in a way, we were reading the book together.

New books are pristine and silent; used books arrive already haunted. Coffee rings mark where someone's afternoon slowed down. A pressed leaf falls out of a poetry collection—who pressed it, and why that page? Bookstores that sell secondhand volumes are really selling these ghosts, this residue of attention.

We think of reading as solitary, but every battered paperback argues otherwise. Attention leaves traces. Somewhere out there, people are inheriting my old underlines and finding them obvious, or wrong, or moving. I like that thought. The margins are full of people who cared enough to talk back to a page—and the page, patient as ever, absorbed all of it without complaint, and kept every secret.
